meta.title: VIETNAM FOOD TOUR: A day eating in Saigon (Ho Chi Minh City)
meta.description:
I spent the day eating my way through Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, stopping at local markets, neighborhood food stalls, and some of my favorite spots to experience the flavors that make Saigon one of the world's greatest food cities.

Since moving to Vietnam, one of my biggest goals has been to deepen my understanding of Vietnamese cuisine by eating like a local, learning the stories behind each dish, and sharing that journey with you. 

If you're planning a trip to Vietnam or simply love Vietnamese food, I hope this video gives you a taste of what makes this city so special.

If you enjoyed the video, don't forget to like, subscribe, and leave a comment letting me know what city or dish I should explore next.

📍Location: Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon), Vietnam

Follow along:Instagram: @dvdnguyen
Substack: https://substack.com/@dvdnguyen
TikTok: @dvdnguyen

comments.author: @zeyjin8852
comments.text:
Vietnamese people give me the impression of having a mentality very similar to what China was like about ten years ago: a strong sense of insecurity and inferiority, combined with the belief that they have somehow won every war they have fought. Even now, many of them still seem to believe that they “won” both the Vietnam War and the Sino-Vietnamese War. It feels like a kind of arrogance that grows out of insecurity.

Another thing is that when they look at their own culture, they often seem to deliberately ignore how much of it actually came from elsewhere. A large part of Vietnamese culture historically came from China, and many foods and cultural influences also came from China or France. Even much of what is considered traditional Vietnamese culture was heavily influenced by China, yet they often seem to intentionally downplay or ignore that connection.

There is also an excessive degree of nationalism. They act as though their country is exceptionally powerful or impressive, while forgetting that Vietnam is ultimately a relatively small and weak country in Southeast Asia. Many aspects of its political system, national traditions, and culture were influenced by or derived from other countries, and much of its modern civilization, industrialization, and modernization also came through outside influence.

What I find striking is this combination of insecurity and overconfidence: an almost baseless sense of superiority that seems to be produced by a deeper sense of inferiority.
